claims.text: The coating has a dual-phase microstructure containing distinct FCC and BCC regions.
The FCC/BCC interphase boundaries in the initial coating are relatively coherent.
Controlled heat treatments or minor compositional adjustments can vary interphase-boundary coherency and interface characteristics.
Coherent FCC/BCC interphase boundaries act as barriers to dislocation motion.
Coherent interphase boundaries act as effective dislocation-pinning sites.
Coherent interphase boundaries promote load partitioning between the FCC and BCC phases.
Impeded dislocation glide and interphase load partitioning delay the onset of creep deformation.
Impeded dislocation glide and interphase load partitioning reduce the creep deformation rate.
Coatings with optimized coherent interphase boundaries will have lower creep rates than coatings with disrupted or less coherent interfaces.
Coatings with optimized coherent interphase boundaries will resist plastic deformation better than coatings with disrupted or less coherent interfaces.
The proposed mechanism operates under high-temperature, long-duration sustained loading where creep is the dominant deformation mechanism.
The magnitude of creep-rate reduction may vary with processing parameters and alloy composition.

Failure to observe a statistically significant reduction in both creep rate and dislocation activity for coherent-interface coatings relative to disrupted-interface controls under identical conditions would falsify the hypothesis.
